formal.statement: theorem Int.fib_rec : ((x0 : Int) -> Eq.{1} Int (Int.fib (Int.add x0 (Int.ofNat (AxNat.succ (AxNat.succ AxNat.zero))))) (Int.add (Int.fib (Int.add x0 Int.one)) (Int.fib x0)))

notes:
Three cases, and only one of them does algebra.
  n >= 0 (ofNat a): every index reduces -- add (ofNat a) (ofNat 2) is definitionally ofNat (succ (succ a)) -- so the whole goal is Nat.fib_add_two pushed through IntDev::nat_eq_to_int. One line.
  n = -1 and n = -2: 1 = 0 + 1 and 0 = 1 + (-1). Both sides are closed terms, so d.irefl reads at the goal and no lemma is used at all. The magnitudes are fib 1 and fib 2, which is why walking them is cheap.
  n <= -3 (negSucc (succ (succ j))): with s := (-1)^j and F1,F2,F3 the natural Fibonacci values at j+1, j+2, j+3, Int.fib's own negSucc clause makes the goal s*F1 = (-s)*F2 + s*F3. The two sign flips come from pow_neg_one_succ applied twice (the second collapsed by neg_neg), Nat.fib_add_two at succ j supplies F3 = F2 + F1, and left_distrib plus one add_assoc reversal annihilate the (-s)*F2 and s*F2 terms.

Three small helpers the integer prelude lacked and this needed: neg_mul (it carries mul_neg), neg_add_cancel (it carries add_neg) and zero_add (it carries add_zero).

Accepted by the kernel on the first attempt.

statement: fib (n + 2) = fib (n + 1) + fib n for every INTEGER n, negative ones included. Nat.fib_add_two is the natural-number half and says nothing below 0, and Int.fib's negSucc clause is a definition rather than a recurrence, so before this nothing in the development related fib(-k-1) to its neighbours.
title: Int.fib_rec -- the Fibonacci recurrence at EVERY integer index
